units.title: The going up offering, the model
units.digest: Yahweh calls Moshe from the Tent he cannot enter and gives the first instruction: how anyone in Yisrael brings near a going up offering. A whole male from the herd or the flock, or a bird: the offerer leans a hand, slaughters, skins and washes; the priests dash the blood and turn it all into smoke, an aroma of rest to Yahweh. The offerings that follow refer back to this model.

meeting.gloss: meeting; a set time or place for meeting
meeting.echo: Lev 23:2 — the same word, plural, names the meeting times: the Tent and the calendar share one root

whole.example: a whole male he shall bring near
whole.echo: Gen 6:9; 17:1 — the same word describes Noaḥ, and what Avraham is told to be before Yahweh

acceptance.echo: Mal 1:8–10 — a governor would not accept blind or lame animals; neither will Yahweh accept them

dash.gloss: dash, throw (a liquid) in a mass
dash.example: dash the blood against the altar all around

cut-up.gloss: cut up limb by limb; the pieces
cut-up.example: cut it up into its pieces

fatty-pieces.example: the head and the fatty pieces
fatty-pieces.echo: Lev 8:20 — the ordination ram's head, pieces and fatty pieces go up in smoke the same way

legs.example: its entrails and its legs he shall wash

tail-end.gloss: a bird's tail end (disputed; others read crop)
tail-end.example: remove its tail end with its feathers

units.title: The grain offering
units.digest: The grain offering is fine flour with oil and frankincense, raw or baked. The priest burns a token handful on the altar, and the rest belongs to Aharon and his sons as most holy. No leaven or honey goes on the altar, and every offering is salted with the salt of the covenant.

units.title: The peace offering
units.digest: The peace offering comes from the herd or the flock, male or female. As with the going up offering, the offerer lays a hand on it and the blood goes on the altar, but only the fat around the inner organs is burned. The chapter ends with a lasting rule: Israel eats no fat and no blood.

units.title: Purification for unwitting wrong
units.digest: When someone sins without meaning to, a sin offering is due, graded by who sinned: the anointed priest, the whole community, a leader, or an ordinary person. Its blood goes further in the more serious cases, as far as the veil. Then come cases of withheld testimony, unnoticed impurity and rash oaths, where the offering is scaled to what the person can afford.

units.title: Guilt offerings
units.digest: Someone who misuses what belongs to Yahweh's holy things, even unknowingly, brings a ram and repays the loss plus a fifth. The same holds for wronging a neighbour by deceit, theft or a false oath: restore what was taken, add a fifth, and bring the ram. Wrong against a neighbour is also unfaithfulness to Yahweh.

units.title: The instruction for each offering
units.digest: Instructions to the priests for each offering already described: the fire on the altar never goes out, and each offering has its own handling. Most of the rules settle which portions the priests eat, where, and who may eat the peace offering. A closing line says these were commanded at Sinai.

units.title: Ordination of Aharon and sons
units.digest: Moshe does what Yahweh commanded in Exodus 29. Before the whole community he washes Aharon and his sons, dresses them, anoints the Tent and Aharon, and offers the ordination sacrifices, putting blood on their right ear, thumb and big toe. They stay at the Tent's entrance for seven days.

units.title: The eighth day
units.digest: On the eighth day Aharon offers for himself and for the people for the first time. When he and Moshe come out and bless the people, Yahweh's glory appears to all, and fire comes out from Yahweh and consumes the offering. The people shout and fall on their faces.

units.title: Nadab and Abihu
units.digest: Nadab and Abihu offer fire Yahweh had not commanded, and fire comes out from Yahweh and consumes them. Aharon is silent, the priests may not mourn in the usual way, and Aharon is told to separate holy from common and clean from unclean. The chapter ends with a dispute over an uneaten sin offering, which Moshe accepts.

units.title: Animals clean and unclean
units.digest: Which animals Israel may eat: land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, water creatures with fins and scales, certain birds and winged insects. Touching their carcasses makes a person unclean until evening. The reason given is holiness: "be holy, because I am holy."

units.title: After childbirth
units.digest: After childbirth a mother is unclean for seven days for a boy, fourteen for a girl, and waits longer before she may touch holy things. At the end she brings a going up offering and a sin offering, and the priest covers for her. A poor mother may bring two birds.

units.title: Flaking in skin and cloth
units.digest: A sore, swelling or patch on the skin is shown to the priest, who examines it, sometimes isolates the person for seven days, and declares it clean or unclean. Someone declared unclean tears their clothes, cries "Unclean!" and lives outside the camp. Mould in cloth or leather is judged the same way.

units.title: Cleansing from flaking; the house
units.digest: The person healed of flaking is restored in stages: two birds and running water outside the camp, washing and shaving, then offerings on the eighth day with blood and oil on ear, thumb and toe. A poorer person brings less. A house with spreading mould is inspected, repaired or torn down, and then cleansed.

units.title: Bodily discharges
units.digest: Discharges from the body make a person unclean, along with whatever they lie or sit on: an abnormal discharge, an emission of semen, menstruation, prolonged bleeding. Washing and waiting end most of these, and the abnormal ones need offerings on the eighth day. The aim is stated at the end: Israel's uncleanness must not defile Yahweh's dwelling among them.

units.title: The Day of Coverings
units.digest: After his sons' deaths, Aharon is told how and when he may enter behind the veil. Once a year he purifies the inner sanctuary, the Tent and the altar with the blood of a bull and a goat, then confesses Israel's sins over a second goat and sends it into the wilderness. Israel rests and humbles itself, and is made clean before Yahweh.

units.title: Blood and slaughter
units.digest: Any ox, sheep or goat that is slaughtered must be brought to the Tent as an offering, not killed elsewhere or offered to goat-demons. No one, Israelite or resident foreigner, may eat blood, because the life is in the blood and Yahweh gave it on the altar to cover. The blood of game is poured out and covered with earth.

units.title: Forbidden unions
units.digest: Israel must not live as Egypt and Canaan do but by Yahweh's rules, which give life. A list follows of forbidden unions with close relatives, along with other forbidden practices, including giving children to Molek. The land vomited out the nations who did these things and will do the same to Israel.

units.title: "Be holy"
units.digest: "Be holy, because I, Yahweh your God, am holy." Holiness covers parents, Sabbath, idols and offerings, but also leaving the edges of the harvest, paying workers on time, fair courts, honest weights, the deaf and the blind, the elderly and the foreigner. At the centre: love your neighbour as yourself, and love the foreigner too.

units.title: Penalties for the same wrongs
units.digest: The wrongs of chapter 18 return with their penalties: giving a child to Molek, consulting mediums, cursing parents, and the forbidden unions. Some are punished by death, others by being cut off or dying childless. Yahweh calls Israel to be holy and separate, as he has separated them from the nations.

units.title: The holiness of priests
units.digest: Priests may mourn only their closest kin, must keep their marriages within set limits, and must not profane themselves. The high priest is held to more: no mourning even for parents, and marriage only to a virgin of his people. A descendant of Aharon with a physical defect may eat the holy food but may not approach the altar.

units.title: Holy gifts and acceptable offerings
units.digest: Priests must not touch holy food while unclean, and only their households may eat it. Offerings must be without defect, with specific defects listed. Yahweh's holy name must not be profaned: he makes Israel holy and brought them out of Egypt.

units.title: The appointed times
units.digest: Yahweh's appointed times: the weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, the first sheaf, the Feast of Weeks fifty days later, then in the seventh month the trumpet day, the Day of Coverings and the Feast of Booths. Each has its offerings and days of rest, and Booths recalls the wilderness shelters.

units.title: Lamp, bread and the blasphemer
units.digest: Pure oil keeps the lamp burning before Yahweh, and twelve loaves are set out each Sabbath. Then a man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father curses the Name in a fight, and Yahweh gives the verdict: the community stones him outside the camp. Life for life, injury for injury, and one law for the foreigner and the native.

units.title: The seventh year and the Jubilee
units.digest: In the land, every seventh year the land itself rests: no sowing or pruning, and the yield is for everyone to eat. After seven of those cycles, the fiftieth year is the Jubilee, proclaimed with a horn on the Day of Coverings, when each person returns to their family land. Yahweh promises enough to eat in the years of rest.

units.title: Redeeming land and kin
units.digest: The land is Yahweh's, so it cannot be sold for good; Israel lives on it as foreigners and tenants. When someone grows poor and sells land or even themselves, the nearest relative should redeem them, and the Jubilee restores them anyway. Israelites are Yahweh's servants, brought out of Egypt, so they must not be held as slaves.

units.title: Blessings and curses
units.digest: Keep no idols and keep Yahweh's Sabbaths. If Israel walks in his laws, there will be rain, harvest, peace, and Yahweh will walk among them. If they refuse, five rounds of punishment grow worse, ending in exile while the land enjoys its Sabbaths. Yet if they confess, Yahweh will remember his covenant with their ancestors.

units.title: Vows and valuations
units.digest: People, animals, houses and fields can be dedicated to Yahweh by a vow, each with a set value in silver, and most can be redeemed by paying the value plus a fifth. Firstborn animals, things devoted to destruction, and the tithe already belong to Yahweh. A closing line says these were commanded at Sinai.
